title: Why action-reaction forces don’t cancel
canonical_question: Why don’t the equal and opposite forces of a third-law pair cancel each other out?
summary: Forces cancel only when they act on the same object, but a third-law pair acts on two different bodies.
Because the pair is split across two bodies, each body can accelerate under the single force it feels.

reuse.rationale: Authored fixture node for the E05 registry.

sections.heading: They act on different bodies
sections.body_md: Forces cancel only when they act on the same object, but a third-law pair acts on two different bodies. Your push on a cart and the cart’s push on you affect different things, so neither is cancelled. Each force does its work on its own body.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.body_md: Because the pair is split across two bodies, each body can accelerate under the single force it feels. If the forces were on one body they would cancel and nothing would move. The split is exactly what lets interactions produce motion.

key_points: Paired forces act on different bodies.
The split lets each body accelerate.
core.bridge_to_parent: It explains a subtlety of the objective without listing pairs.
